title: VKH Syndrome: The Comprehensive Clinical Masterguide
summary: A multisystemic, T-cell mediated autoimmune attack on melanocyte-containing tissues, primarily affecting the eyes, ears, meninges, and skin. This guide covers the evolution from the prodromal phase to chronic recurrent granulomatous inflammation.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome is a bilateral, granulomatous panuveitis associated with extraocular manifestations involving the auditory, neurological, and integumentary systems. It is driven by a T-cell mediated autoimmune response against tyrosinase-related proteins in melanocytes.

rows: Viral-like illness, headache, meningismus, tinnitus, CSF pleocytosis.
Bilateral exudative RD, thickened choroid, optic disc hyperemia.
Sunset glow fundus, Sugiura sign (perilimbic vitiligo), skin changes.
Smouldering granulomatous anterior uveitis, mutton-fat KPs, Busacca nodules.
Bilateral Ocular + EITHER Neuro/Auditory OR Integumentary signs.
Bilateral Ocular signs ONLY (Isolated Ocular VKH).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Posterior Segment: Multifocal serous RDs, 'clover-leaf' fluid patterns.
Optic Nerve: Hyperemia and edema (Acute phase).
Fundus: 'Sunset Glow' (depigmentation revealing orange-red choroid).
Anterior Segment: Mutton-fat KPs, Koeppe/Busacca nodules.
Dalén-Fuchs Nodules: Small yellow-white granulomatous lesions (less common than SO).

sections.title: Essential Diagnostic Imaging
content: 1. OCT: Shows subretinal fluid, bacillary layer detachment, and choroidal thickening.
2. FFA: Pinpoint leaks ('Starry Sky') in early phase; pooling in late phase.
3. ICG: Early/mid-phase hypofluorescent spots (HDDs), fuzzy choroidal vessels.
4. B-Scan: Diffuse low-to-medium reflective choroidal thickening; no posterior scleritis 'T-sign'.

rows: History of penetrating trauma or surgery in the 'exciting' eye.
Pain with eye movement, T-sign on USG, usually unilateral.
Hilar lymphadenopathy on CXR, elevated ACE/Lysozyme.
Placoid lesions, rapid resolution, minimal vitreous reaction.

sections.title: Acute Phase Management Protocol
content: Step 1: IV Methylprednisolone (1g/day) for 3 days for severe cases.
Step 2: Transition to Oral Prednisolone (1-1.5 mg/kg/day).
Step 3: Ultra-slow taper (minimum 6-12 months total duration).
Step 4: Cycloplegics and topical steroids for anterior segment activity.

content.explanation: S: Sugiura Sign (Perilimbic vitiligo); U: Uveitis (Bilateral/Granulomatous); N: Neurological (Meningismus); S: Subretinal fluid; E: Ears (Tinnitus); T: Tegumentary (Vitiligo/Poliosis).

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Treatment Pitfalls
content: Rapid steroid taper: High risk of transitioning to chronic-recurrent stage.
Under-recognizing 'smouldering' activity: Persistent choroidal thickening on EDI-OCT.
Steroid-induced Glaucoma/Cataract: Must monitor IOP and lens status at every visit.
Neurological deficits: May require neurology co-management and MRI.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Fellow
content: Early IMT initiation is now preferred (as per MUST trial principles) to prevent 'sunset glow' fundus.
The Sugiura Sign is the earliest integumentary sign (appears ~1 month).
EDI-OCT is the most sensitive non-invasive tool to monitor disease activity.
Avoid intravitreal steroid implants in the acute phase before systemic control is achieved.

sections.title: Prognostic Indicators
sections.content: Good visual prognosis (20/40 or better) is achievable in >70% of patients if treated aggressively within the first 2 weeks of symptoms. Poorer outcomes are linked to older age, more frequent recurrences, and delayed start of immunosuppression.

sections.title: Recent Landmark Insights
content: Bacillary Layer Detachment (BLD): Recognized on OCT as a split at the inner segment myoid, distinct from subretinal fluid.
The Role of IL-17: Newer studies suggest Th17 cells are pivotal in the chronic phase, suggesting potential for Secukinumab in refractory cases.
First-line IMT: Growing evidence supports starting Mycophenolate Mofetil concurrently with steroids in the acute phase.
